summary: This experimental memo documents a Type of Service value that requests maximum physical link security, an addition to the types of service in RFC 1349. It was replaced by RFC 2474.

eli5.summary: A packet can carry a note saying how it wants to be treated. This paper adds a note meaning, send me over the most secure wires you have.

questions: physical link security type of service
subtitle: A Type of Service marking for routing over more physically secure network links.

tldr.problem: Traffic on the Internet can be observed by outside adversaries, enabling traffic analysis (deducing activities from packet flow statistics) and data interception, even if the data itself is encrypted at higher layers.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC proposes using a Type of Service value (15 in decimal) to request that packets be routed through more physically secure links. Routers implementing TOS-based routing can assign costs to links based on their physical security characteristics and route these marked packets accordingly.
tldr.outcome: The proposal showed that IP networks could be requested to optimize for security. However, it was replaced by RFC 2474, which defined QoS and DSCP classes. This particular approach did not become widely used.

today: RFC 1455 was replaced by RFC 2474, which defined Quality of Service (QoS) and Differentiated Services Code Point (DSCP) classes. While the physical-link-security approach proposed here was not widely deployed, modern QoS mechanisms provide ways to request special handling of packets.

sections.title: Link Security as a Routing Preference
sections.content:
Internet Protocol packets must carry their source and destination addresses in clear text so that routers can forward them. This makes even encrypted data subject to traffic analysis: an observer watching the network flow can deduce what hosts are communicating and when, even if they cannot read the content of the packets.

This RFC proposes a new Type of Service (TOS) value to let applications request that packets be routed through more physically secure links. The value 15 (binary 1111, chosen for maximum difference from other TOS values) requests the network to use routes that are harder for external observers to monitor. This provides protection against traffic analysis and adds a layer of confidentiality, especially useful when end-to-end encryption is not available.
sections.eli5: Letters have to show their addresses so mail carriers can deliver them, but that means anyone watching can see who is mailing to whom. This RFC suggests a way to ask the network to send your packets through the hardest-to-spy-on routes.

sections.title: Why Physical Link Security Matters
sections.content:
Physical communication links differ widely in their susceptibility to eavesdropping. Fiber optic cables are harder to tap than copper wires. Secure land lines in pressurized conduit with alarms are harder to access than open lines. Encrypted links are better than unencrypted ones. Point-to-point links are more secure than broadcast media like Ethernet. Spread spectrum radio is harder to intercept than normal broadcast.

The RFC lists examples: fiber optic land lines are harder to tap; satellite downlinks with large coverage areas are easier to intercept; encrypted links dominate all other protections in security. By requesting routes through more secure links, even though there is no guaranteed service level, applications and users can improve their protection against traffic analysis and data interception.

The RFC acknowledges that in 1993 most of the Internet did not implement TOS-based routing, and that resource reservation or policy routing would be needed for true guarantees. However, it argues that users who need protection should be able to request higher physical security as a preference.
sections.eli5: Some cables are easier to spy on than others. Fiber is hard to tap. Encrypted links are best. By labeling packets with this special mark, the network tries to use harder-to-spy-on routes, though it cannot guarantee it.

sections.title: Implementation in Routing Systems
sections.content:
Routers that support TOS-based routing (such as OSPF routers) can implement this by assigning a cost to each link based on its physical security. The costs should reflect the relative probability that each link could be intercepted. A strongly encrypted link with secure key distribution might have cost 1; a satellite link cost 32; a typical broadcast media cost 8 or 12.

The RFC notes that using such costs could cause packets to take longer, more circuitous routes than normal routing. However, if costs are set proportionally to interception probability, the longer path through more secure links is more secure overall than a shorter path through less secure links. The RFC also cautions that both links and routers must be considered for security, since a path through many insecure routers may be worse than a path through fewer secure routers.

One limitation: standard routing algorithms sum link costs, but for security a product of probabilities would be more mathematically correct. However, the RFC notes this same issue affects other TOS types like high reliability, and summing costs is an adequate approximation.
sections.eli5: A router can assign a number to each link saying how hard it is to spy on. Shorter paths are faster but less secure; longer paths through secure links take more time but are safer. The router picks the secure route if that's what the packet asks for.

sections.title: Security and Limitations
sections.content:
The proposal acknowledges important limitations: it does not provide guaranteed service levels, only a preference. Even in 1993, most of the Internet did not implement TOS-based routing, so the marking could not be honored end-to-end. A network path might include links and routers where TOS routing is not supported.

Furthermore, the approach defends against traffic analysis by external observers, but cannot protect against an adversary with inside access to the network. A sophisticated attacker with access to router equipment can still see all traffic regardless of the path chosen. The RFC is honest about this: it says use of more secure physical links will make observation by entities outside the network more difficult, not impossible.

The RFC correctly frames this as a best-effort mechanism: users who need protection from traffic analysis or who cannot use end-to-end encryption (for example, in countries that restrict encryption) can request this service, understanding that the network will do its best but cannot guarantee anything.
sections.eli5: This doesn't promise complete security, just that the network will try to use safer routes if it can. It only protects against outsiders spying on the wires, not against someone with access to the router equipment. It's helpful, but not a guarantee.
